bull_bear.body:
- Listing / regulatory compliance lapses — Not a hypothetical: the Board's Report discloses under 'PENALTIES / FINES' that during FY2025-26 the Company incurred penalties imposed by BSE Limited for delayed compliance with certain provisions of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 and Stock Exchange requirements. The Board characterises the matters as 'specific and procedural in nature', but repeated delays carry escalating exchange penalties and reputational cost for a listed NBFC.
- Change in regulatory norms — Named explicitly in the MD&A forward-looking caveat as one of the risks and uncertainties to which the discussion is subject. As an RBI-regulated NBFC the Company's operations, capital and lending activity are governed by RBI directions issued for NBFCs 'from time to time', so a change in those directions flows directly into the business.
- Execution risk inherent to the growth strategy — The MD&A states the forward-looking statements involve risks and uncertainties 'including but not limited to the risks inherent to Company's growth strategy', and warns that actual results could differ materially.
- Sensitivity to economic conditions and the macro cycle — Named in the MD&A forward-looking caveat alongside 'other incidental factors'. Management's own outlook rests on macro conditions — supportive liquidity, lower bond yields and hence lower NBFC borrowing costs — so an adverse turn in those conditions reverses the stated funding-cost and margin tailwind.
- Global macro and financial-market instability — The MD&A economic overview enumerates still-elevated inflation, tight monetary and financial conditions, escalating geopolitical tensions, rising geo-economic fragmentation, disruptions in key global shipping routes, high public debt burdens and financial stability risks, with global financial markets 'on edge' and recurrent bouts of volatility around central-bank policy trajectories.
- Sovereign fiscal position — Management flags that India's high government capital spending has pushed the fiscal deficit to 4.4% of GDP and that combined debt-to-GDP levels remain above pre-pandemic levels — a constraint on the supportive-liquidity and low-bond-yield assumption underpinning its own funding-cost outlook.
- No access to public deposits as a funding source — The Company is a non-deposit-taking NBFC registered with the RBI and is prohibited from accepting public deposits; it accepted none during the year and had no public deposit outstanding as at 31 March 2026. Funding must therefore come from equity and borrowings rather than low-cost retail deposits.

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body:
- Management expects the NBFC sector in India to benefit from a favourable macroeconomic environment in FY 2025-26, with liquidity conditions expected to remain supportive for financial institutions despite a fiscal deficit pushed to 4.4% of GDP and debt-to-GDP above pre-pandemic levels
- The RBI's higher-than-expected dividend payout of Rs 2.87 trillion is flagged as a key positive: it strengthens the government's fiscal position, reduces second-half market borrowing needs and is likely to keep bond yields lower
- Lower bond yields are expected to translate into reduced borrowing costs for NBFCs, which management says should improve funding access and profitability margins
- Indian economy described as growing 7.7% in FY 2025-26, underpinned by strong investment activity amid subdued external demand, with manufacturing and services the key supply-side drivers and agriculture slowed by uneven, deficient monsoon rainfall
- Growth outlook described as buoyant on sustained government capital expenditure with fiscal consolidation, strong corporate balance sheets, rising capacity utilisation and double-digit credit growth
- Global backdrop flagged as a countervailing factor — elevated inflation, tight monetary and financial conditions, geopolitical tensions, geo-economic fragmentation, shipping-route disruption, high public debt and financial stability risks keeping global financial markets volatile
